items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And even we played a lot of fast tunes when he and Lockjaw Davis had the quintet.

ctx.x: Man, I listened to that and I’m wondering if you ever were in a situation on a record like that and they’re counting off the tune like that, and you’re going, oh please, not that fast. That sounded awful fast to me.

Believe it or not, I’m in a situation now — I still like to play fast but not as often. But this was the thing in Chicago, I don’t know why, all the tenor players liked to play fast, which is what I worked with mostly. Gene Ammons loved to play fast and way up there. But he never would record that fast. Johnny Griffin still plays a mile a minute. He’s from Chicago also, and we worked together a few times, and I think every other tune was like that. And even we played a lot of fast tunes when he and Lockjaw Davis…
got to think of something meaningful to play. But when you play fast like that, you know you can put your exercises together so to speak, you know the changes.

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And people like that, Coleman Hawkins played the Beehive, Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis, Sonny Stitt, just about everybody you can name. And they all came without groups.

ctx.x: Did you ever have occasion in those situations where someone would bring in a four page piece of music for the piano player, and you’re going “oh God, where’s the chord symbols?”

Oh, I feel the same way. I was never a fast sight reader. But you know as a kid I learned how to read music but it’s something that, you have to keep doing it. Once you stop, you’re going to not do it as well. And I stopped for years, because I went to the small band type way of playing. My reading was probably best right after high school and my first year of Roosevelt College. I was with this local big band, the one I was talking about that Gene Ammons played in. It was like the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band of…

blues, maybe that’s something in the back of my mind as to why I don’t have that much music. I have some tunes you know. Occasionally I let them work on a bebop tune and let an ensemble do it, but other than that I just sort of got away from it. I was never that interested in getting back to it. I was never interested; and doing studio work, which is probably the most lucrative part of the business you know. Like look at the studio musicians now, even those into retirement, man they have pensions in five and six…
